title: The $27,000 Problem: Musasa’s Broken Pump and the Cost of Waiting
subtitle: Water trucks brought relief to Musasa in July. Residents still wanted the pump repaired.
excerpt: In June, a Musasa resident described spending 210,000 Burundian francs a month on water after a pump failure. Emergency deliveries arrived in July. Residents were still asking for the pump to be repaired.

content.text: In June 2026, Sifa told SOS Médias Burundi that she was paying about 210,000 Burundian francs a month for water. Sifa lived in Musasa refugee camp in northern Burundi. There were ten people in her household, she said. She used her World Food Programme assistance to buy water. That left little for meals or healthcare. Local sources told the outlet it would cost about $27,000 to replace the broken pump motor. For more than six months, the camp’s more than 9,000 Congolese refugees had lacked a regular supply of drinking water.

In July, SOS Médias Burundi reported that UNHCR started trucking water from Gasorwe, filling the tanks connected to the camp taps. Residents said their water bills had fallen. They worried that a fuel shortage might interrupt deliveries and wanted the pump repaired, with reliable electricity to run it.

In July 2026, SOS Médias Burundi reported another lengthy disruption in water supply in Uganda's Nakivale settlement. Some residents were travelling roughly eight kilometres to Lake Nakivale; others purchased water delivered by bicycle. A medical source quoted by the outlet described patients with signs of cholera and typhoid. The hospital itself lacked drinking water. UNHCR staff told the outlet they lacked money for basic supplies.

Radio Ergo documented a similar breakdown in Hagadera camp in Kenya's Dadaab complex in March 2026. Camp officials stated that at least four boreholes had broken down in the preceding year without proper repairs. The deputy chairman, Abukar Sheikh Abdullahi, said the administration could not afford the repairs. Nimo, a resident interviewed by the outlet, had food in the house but no water to cook it.

content.alt: People collecting water in containers at a communal water point
content.caption: People collect water at a communal supply point. Editorial stock photograph.

content.text: In November 2025, UNHCR projected that it would end the year with $3.9 billion available, almost a quarter less than in 2024. Early pledges for 2026 reached about $1.5 billion, nearly 18% of projected needs, with further contributions expected. These agency-wide figures do not tell us how much money was available for the repair of Musasa's water system.

In May 2025, WFP warned that refugees it was supporting in Kenya would receive only 28% of a full in-kind ration from June, and that cash assistance would stop unless more funding arrived. A family buying water from its food allowance has less left for meals. Those who cannot buy water must spend time collecting it or cut back on washing.
Building for a settlement that stays

In Forced Migration Review, Lucy Earle, Kate Crawford and Margarita Garfias Royo describe government resistance to permanent infrastructure at Zaatari in Jordan, and the cost of trucking water in. Networks were operating by mid-2019, but in a 2022 survey, 30% of households reported insufficient water. People the researchers spoke to said that summer trucking was still required.

content.alt: Families with containers beside a large water tank
content.caption: Families collect water beside a storage tank. Editorial stock photograph.

content.text: The authors were not able to obtain a reliable breakdown of Zaatari's water system costs. Evaluations showed that budgets for the wider Jordan water, sanitation and hygiene programme were about $355 million for 2013-2017 and $139 million for 2018-2022, with little detail on expenditure. Without spending records for Zaatari alone, the authors could not compare the cost of trucking water with the cost of a permanent network.

The University of Colorado Boulder describes a system for detecting faults earlier. The Drought Resilience Impact Platform (DRIP) uses satellite-connected sensors, data on groundwater and rainfall and drought forecasts. The project involves the Millennium Water Alliance and Virridy, as well as local institutions. The partners use the readings to plan maintenance and water-service contracts.

A sensor cannot provide a replacement motor, arrange its delivery or fund the repair technician. For a settlement considering the same approach: who receives the alert, who is responsible for the repair, and what money can that person spend without waiting for another emergency appeal?

Kenya’s Shirika Plan, launched in March 2025, aims to integrate refugee services into national and local systems. At the launch of the plan, UNHCR's Filippo Grandi stressed that local authorities need resources to serve refugees and host communities. Each site still needs to establish who can pay for local repairs.

July's deliveries gave residents water while they continued to ask for the pump to be repaired. There will be another bill after the motor: electricity, worn parts and a technician’s time. A water plan needs money for those bills and someone with the authority to spend it. In Musasa, families like Sifa’s had been covering the shortfall.
